title: Course notes
text:
Welcome to this course! These notes are a reference: the main way through the course is the slides and live demos, and every exercise is on the slides too. Use the notes afterwards to revisit the detail, copy commands and check the answers.
The course introduces practical habits that make your research easier to re-run, understand and share, whether you work in R, Python or spreadsheets.
By the end of this course you will be able to:

Organise a project into raw data, processed data, code and outputs, and explain why raw data is never edited.
Write a README and a data dictionary that help others understand and use your project.
Explain why Quarto helps reproducibility, and build a report that updates when the data changes.
Explain why environments matter, and record the software a project needs so it can be re-run on another computer.
Check a dataset against the Q-FAIR principles, and know where to find out more about sharing data.



How to read this document

Small snippets of code are shown in a grey box like this:
cat("Hello!")
When the code is run, its output is shown below it, marked with a vertical red line:

cat("Hello!")

Hello!


Larger pieces of code are shown as scripts with a filename:


script.R

name <- "Jean Golding"
cat("Hello,", name, "!")

Commands to run in a terminal look like this:


Terminal/Command Prompt

Rscript script.R

At the end of each section there is an exercise, which is also shown on the slides. Here, exercises are shown in blue boxes, followed by a yellow box that contains the answer. Try each exercise yourself before looking at the answer.






NoteExercise



This is an exercise. Click the box below to see the answer.








CautionAnswer (click to open)





This is the answer.



Important points are highlighted in green boxes like this one:






TipKey points



These are important concepts and technical notes.





Please follow our installation instructions before the course. You will also need the following.
Quarto. We use Quarto to build reports. RStudio and Positron include it, so if you use either you probably don’t need to install anything. To check, open a .qmd file and look for the Render button. Otherwise, install Quarto for your operating system (VS Code users also need the Quarto extension). Use version 1.4 or later: quarto --version in a terminal shows which you have.
The example folder. Download the example folder and unzip it. It has the data and files we use as we go. If something doesn’t work, the finished/ folder inside it has the ready-made result.
For Section 3. Python users need uv, and R users need the renv package. If you use Excel, you don’t need to install anything extra.






Note



This course is for people who use R, Python or spreadsheets such as Excel. The ideas are the same for everyone, and the slides flag where Excel users do something different. Where the steps differ, you will see tabs: click the one that matches how you work. Commands for the terminal are shown as code, and you can run them in the terminal built in to your IDE or in a separate terminal window.

title: Course notes
text:
1.1 Why bother?
A project that has grown organically tends to look like a folder full of files called data.csv, data_final.csv, analysis2.R and analysis_NEW.py. This causes three problems:

Hard to maintain: one change near the start breaks everything downstream.
Hard to run somewhere else: a new laptop, an HPC cluster or a colleague’s machine, and the code breaks.
Hard to understand: after a holiday you can’t remember which file to run first.

Making a project more reproducible helps you first and others second:

Saving your future self: write code as if someone else will use it, because in six months that someone is you.
Speed: a project set up as a pipeline can be re-run quickly when the data or a reviewer’s comment changes.
Confidence: you understand how the work fits together, and where it might fail.
Publication and jobs: sharing code and data is an increasingly common requirement, and tidy work is easy to trust.







TipYou don’t need everything



How much structure a project needs is a judgement call. A small one-off analysis may not need all of this. Aim for what is useful, not what is perfect.

title: Course notes
text:
1.2 A Messy Example
my_project/
├── data.csv
├── data_final.csv
├── data_final_v2.csv
├── explore.ipynb
├── clean_data.py
├── analysis.py
├── analysis_OLD.py
├── fig1.png
└── results.xlsx
Questions to ask of this layout:

Which data file is the original?
Which script should be run first?
Which figure came from which version of the analysis?

This happens naturally. You start by exploring a dataset in a notebook, a script or an Excel sheet. The analysis grows, then a second analysis is added, and it becomes hard to see how you got from the raw data to the results.

title: Course notes
text:
1.3 A Clean Example
my_project/
├── README.md
├── data/
│   ├── raw/          <- original data, never edited
│   └── processed/    <- cleaned data made by your code
├── code/
│   └── 01_clean_data.R
├── report.qmd
└── outputs/
    ├── figures/
    └── tables/
The key ideas are:

A README at the top of the project says what it is and how to use it (see the next section).
Raw data is read-only. Never overwrite your original data file. Save the cleaned version somewhere else.
Code is a pipeline. Each step reads the output of the previous step: raw data -> clean -> analysis -> outputs. Numbering the files shows the order to run them in.
Outputs can be thrown away. Anything in outputs/ and data/processed/ should be re-creatable by running the code.


RPythonExcel / no code




code/01_clean_data.R

raw <- read.csv("data/raw/penguins.csv")

# drop any rows with missing values
clean <- na.omit(raw)

write.csv(clean, "data/processed/penguins_clean.csv", row.names = FALSE)





code/01_clean_data.py

import pandas as pd

raw = pd.read_csv("data/raw/penguins.csv")

# drop any rows with missing values
clean = raw.dropna()

clean.to_csv("data/processed/penguins_clean.csv", index=False)



The same structure works for spreadsheets:

Keep the original file in a data/raw folder and never edit it. Open it, then use Save As to put a working copy in data/processed.
Use one sheet per step, in order, and name them (1_raw, 2_cleaned, 3_results) rather than leaving Sheet1.
Write down in the README what you did to the data at each step, in enough detail that someone else could repeat it. Avoid manual changes you can’t describe.
Put formulas in cells rather than pasting values, so the calculation is visible.










TipTip: where to start a new project



Some IDEs can create a new project with a sensible set of folders for you. Positron, RStudio and VS Code can all start a new project from a menu, and Python tools such as uv init create the starting files from the terminal. Use whatever is quickest, then add the data/ and outputs/ folders.

title: Course notes
text:
Exercise






NoteExercise



Below is the file list for a messy project.
final.xlsx    final_v2.xlsx    notes.txt    plot.png    clean.R    model.R    penguins_raw.csv    penguins_edited.csv

Sketch a clean folder layout for these files.
Which file would you mark as read-only, and why?
In what order would you run the scripts?









CautionAnswer (click to open)





One possible layout:
project/
├── README.md              <- includes the notes from notes.txt
├── data/
│   ├── raw/penguins_raw.csv
│   └── processed/penguins_edited.csv
├── code/
│   ├── 01_clean.R
│   └── 02_model.R
└── outputs/
    ├── plot.png
    └── final.xlsx

See the layout above.
penguins_raw.csv is the original data and should be read-only, as everything else can be remade from it. penguins_edited.csv should be the output of clean.R rather than something edited by hand.
clean.R first, then model.R, because the model needs the cleaned data.

Also, final.xlsx and final_v2.xlsx should be one file, with the history left to version control or the README. Delete or archive the old one.









TipKey points




Separate raw data, processed data, code and outputs.
Never overwrite the raw data.
Think of the analysis as a pipeline that can be re-run from start to finish.
This applies equally to scripts, notebooks and spreadsheets.

title: Course notes
text:
2.1 Types of documentation









Type
Where
Why
Audience




Comments in code
Scripts, notebooks, function docstrings
Explain or justify what isn’t obvious from the code
Other researchers and developers


Files in the repository
README.md
Describe how to use the project
Developers, and people running the code


Data dictionary
A CSV next to the data
Explain what each column means, its units and missing values
Anyone using the data


External documentation
A website or report
Describe what you are doing in less technical terms, with quickstart guides
Users and less technical readers



A good comment says why, not what. # remove outliers > 3 SD, as agreed with the lab is more useful than # remove outliers.

title: Course notes
text:
2.2 README.md
A README is a plain text file in the top folder of the project. It is the first thing someone reads, and it helps you in six months’ time as much as it helps anyone else. It should contain:

Summary: what the project is for, and its status (for example ongoing or complete).
Quickstart: the most important files, and in what order to run them.
Setup: what needs to be installed before running the code.
Contents: a description of what each folder holds.

A README is written in Markdown, which is a simple way of marking up text:
# Penguins analysis

Body measurements of penguins on three islands. **Status:** ongoing.

## Quickstart

1. Put the raw data in `data/raw/`.
2. Run `code/01_clean_data.R`.
3. Render `report.qmd`.

## Setup

Requires R and Quarto (see "Virtual Environments").

## Contents

- `data/raw/` original data (read-only)
- `data/processed/` cleaned data, and its data dictionary
- `code/` analysis scripts
- `outputs/` figures and tables
You can use a README in any project, whether or not you write code. For a spreadsheet project it is the place to record what each sheet does and how the data was collected.

title: Course notes
text:
2.3 Data dictionary
A dataset on its own doesn’t explain itself. What does bill_dep mean? Is body_mass in grams or kilograms? Does a blank mean it wasn’t measured? Write this down in a data dictionary, a small table with one row per column:









column
type
description
units / values




species
text
Penguin species
Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo


island
text
Island where the penguin was observed
Biscoe, Dream, Torgersen


bill_len
number
Bill length
mm


bill_dep
number
Bill depth
mm


flipper_len
number
Flipper length
mm


body_mass
number
Body mass
grams


sex
text
Sex of the penguin
female, male; blank if not recorded


year
number
Year of the study
2007, 2008 or 2009



Save it next to the data (for example data/processed/penguins_clean_dictionary.csv) and refer to it from your README. You can also include a short description of the whole dataset: who collected it, when, how, and any known problems. A dictionary is one of the most valuable things you can write, because only the person who knows the data can.
To make one, copy your column names into a spreadsheet or CSV file, then add columns for the type, a description, and the units or values. Fill them in by hand, and save the file as a CSV next to the data.

title: Course notes
text:
2.4 What is Quarto?
Quarto is a free, open-source tool for writing documents that combine text and code. You write one file (report.qmd). When you render it, the code runs, and the results (numbers, tables and figures) are put into a finished document, such as an HTML page, a PDF or a Word file.
Quarto works with R, Python and other languages, from the IDE you already use. The slides, the notes and the website for this course are all made with Quarto.

title: Course notes
section: 2.5 Why use Quarto for reproducible research?
text:
2.5 Why use Quarto for reproducible research?
A report is often the last step of an analysis, and the easiest place to introduce mistakes: a number is copied from the wrong run, or a figure is from an older version of the data. Quarto removes that step.

No copy and paste. Numbers, tables and figures come straight from the code, so they can’t drift out of sync with the analysis.
Always up to date. If the data changes, render again and the whole report updates.
One source, many outputs. The same file can make HTML, PDF, Word, slides and websites.
Plain text. A .qmd file is easy to share, compare and keep in version control, in any editor.





Without Quarto
With Quarto




1
Run the analysis
Write the report once, with the code in it


2
Copy numbers and plots into a Word document
Render


3
The data changes
The data changes


4
Repeat by hand, and hope you caught every number
Render again

title: Course notes
text:
2.6 Weaving text and analysis together
A Quarto file has four ingredients:

A header with the title and the output format (between two lines of ---).
Text, written in Markdown: headings, paragraphs, lists and links.
Code chunks: R or Python code in a fenced block. When you render, the code runs and its output (a table, a plot) appears underneath.
Inline code: a result inside a sentence, which is recalculated every time you render.


RPythonExcel / no code




report.qmd

---
title: "Penguin report"
format: html
---

## Data

```{r}
clean <- read.csv("data/processed/penguins_clean.csv")

# keep one species: filter out Adelie and Chinstrap
gentoo <- subset(clean, species == "Gentoo")
```

After removing incomplete rows, there are `{r} nrow(clean)` penguins in the data. `{r} nrow(gentoo)` of them are Gentoo penguins.

## Results

The mean body mass of Gentoo penguins was `{r} round(mean(gentoo$body_mass))` g.

```{r}
boxplot(body_mass ~ sex, data = gentoo, ylab = "Body mass (g)")
```





report.qmd

---
title: "Penguin report"
format: html
---

## Data

```{python}
import pandas as pd

clean = pd.read_csv("data/processed/penguins_clean.csv")

# keep one species: filter out Adelie and Chinstrap
gentoo = clean[clean["species"] == "Gentoo"]
```

After removing incomplete rows, there are `{python} len(clean)` penguins in the data. `{python} len(gentoo)` of them are Gentoo penguins.

## Results

The mean body mass of Gentoo penguins was `{python} round(gentoo["body_mass"].mean())` g.

```{python}
gentoo.boxplot(column="body_mass", by="sex")
```

(The plot needs the matplotlib package.)


Quarto can be used for the written part of a project even if your analysis is in a spreadsheet. Save your final table as a CSV, then include it in the report:


report.qmd

---
title: "Penguin report"
format: html
---

Results from the spreadsheet analysis:

```{r}
knitr::kable(read.csv("outputs/tables/results.csv"))
```

This still needs R installed. If you’d rather not use code at all, a README and clearly labelled sheets are the best documentation you can write.

title: Course notes
text:
2.7 When the data changes
Because the numbers in the report come from code, a change in the data flows through to the report:
new data  ->  re-run the cleaning script  ->  render the report  ->  updated report
Every number, table and figure is recalculated, and sentences with inline code update too. There is nothing to copy and paste. This is the main reason to use Quarto for reproducible research: change the data (or the code), not the report.

title: Course notes
text:
2.8 Rendering
Render the report from the terminal, or with the Render button in your IDE:


Terminal/Command Prompt

quarto render report.qmd

The result, report.html, appears next to report.qmd.

title: Course notes
text:
2.9 What else can Quarto do?

Reports in HTML, PDF and Word, with tables, figures and references.
Slides: the slides for this course are a Quarto presentation.
Websites: this course website is built with Quarto.
Papers and books: journal articles, theses and books, with citations and cross-references.

title: Course notes
text:
2.10 Learn more about Quarto

Get started and the guide.
Using code: R, Python and inline code.
Output formats, websites and presentations.
The Quarto gallery: examples to copy from.

title: Course notes
text:
Exercise






NoteExercise



Predict, then check.

Pick a change: a different species, a different column to average, or the “later years” line in the cleaning script.
Write down what you expect to change in the report.
Make the change, render, and compare with your prediction.

If you have a project of your own, write its README and data dictionary too.








CautionAnswer (click to open)






You could say what would change before you rendered, and why.
Only the results changed: no copying and pasting was needed.
A good README answers three questions in the first minute: What is this project and is it finished? If I just want to run it, what do I do first? What do I need installed?
A data dictionary has a plain-English description, units and missing-value codes for every column.










TipKey points




Document at several levels: comments, the README, a data dictionary and external write-ups.
Every project should have a README, and every dataset a data dictionary.
Quarto turns code and text into a report that can be re-created at any time.
If the data changes, render again and the whole report updates.

title: Course notes
text:
3.1 Why do we need environments?
Imagine this sequence:

Last year you wrote an analysis, and it runs, using version 1.2.1 of a package (here, the R package tidyr).
This year you start a new project that needs version 1.3.1, so you update.
You re-run last year’s analysis, and it breaks, or gives different results.





Old project
New project




Program
R 4.3.0
R 4.3.0


tidyr
1.2.1
1.3.1


ggplot2
3.3.5
3.5.0



Your computer has one shared set of packages, so two projects that need different versions can’t both be happy. This happens for several reasons:

Packages change. Functions are renamed, defaults change and bugs are fixed.
Your code depends on them. The same code with a different package version can give a different result.
Other computers differ. A colleague, a new laptop or an HPC cluster will have different versions installed: “it works on my machine”.
Nothing records it. Your project doesn’t say which versions it needs, so nobody can tell what went wrong.

title: Course notes
section: 3.2 What is an environment, and how does it work?
text:
3.2 What is an environment, and how does it work?
An environment is a project’s own set of packages, at the versions it needs. Instead of one shared library for every project, each project has its own, so projects can’t interfere with each other.
Environments work with two things:

A lock file is the recipe: an exact list of packages and versions. It is a small text file, and you keep it with your project.
The environment is what gets built from the lock file: the installed packages, in their own folder. Your code only sees the packages in its own environment.

The environment is disposable: you can delete it, and rebuild it from the lock file whenever you like. The lock file is the thing you keep.




Python
R




Tool
uv
renv


Lock file (keep it)
uv.lock
renv.lock


Environment (disposable)
.venv
renv/library


Rebuild it
uv sync
renv::restore()



Other tools do the same job: venv, conda and pixi for Python, and conda or pixi for R. The idea is the same whichever you use: a file that records what the project needs.

title: Course notes
section: 3.3 Send your project to someone, and it works
text:
3.3 Send your project to someone, and it works
This is the payoff. Because the lock file records exactly what the project needs, you can send your project to a colleague, a reviewer, or yourself on a new laptop, and they can rebuild the same environment with one command:
your project + lock file  ->  colleague rebuilds the environment  ->  same packages, same results

Send: your code, README and lock file (and the data, if you can share it).
Don’t send: the environment itself. It is large, and specific to your computer.

title: Course notes
text:
3.4 What environments don’t cover

They record packages. Also write down the version of R or Python in your README. (uv can pin the Python version; renv records the R version but doesn’t install it.)
The operating system and hardware can still differ.
They don’t include your data.

That is good enough for almost every project. Perfect is not the goal.

title: Course notes
text:
3.5 What if I use Excel?
There are no packages to install, but the software version can still matter: formulas and functions differ between Excel versions, and add-ins vary. Write the program and its version in your README (for example Excel for Microsoft 365, version 2410), along with any add-ins used. The next person then knows what you used, which is the same idea.

title: Course notes
text:
3.6 uv (Python)
uv creates the environment and records the packages for you.


Terminal/Command Prompt

uv init my_project          # create a new project
cd my_project
uv add pandas matplotlib    # install packages and record them
uv run python code/01_clean_data.py   # run a script inside the environment

This creates two files that you keep with your code:

pyproject.toml lists the packages you asked for.
uv.lock records the exact versions installed.

Someone with your project folder can recreate the environment with:


Terminal/Command Prompt

uv sync

title: Course notes
text:
3.7 renv (R)
renv does the same job for R packages. Run these in the R console:
install.packages("renv")   # once, on your computer

renv::init()               # start using renv in this project
install.packages("ggplot2")
renv::snapshot()           # record the packages used in renv.lock
The renv.lock file records the packages and versions. Someone who opens your project can run:
renv::restore()
to install the same versions. renv does not change the version of R itself. To manage that, use a tool such as rig, and record the R version in your README.

title: Course notes
text:
3.8 IDE Vs CLI
Everything above can be done either by typing commands in a terminal (the CLI) or through the menus of your IDE. They do the same thing.








Task
CLI
In an IDE




New Python project with environment
uv init
e.g. Positron: New Folder from Template then choose a Python project with a new environment


Install a package
uv add pandas or install.packages()
Package panel, if your IDE has one


Re-create an environment
uv sync or renv::restore()
Often prompted for when you open the project


Render a report
quarto render report.qmd
The Render button



We recommend learning the CLI commands, because:

they are the same whatever IDE you use, and in instructions you read online;
they work on a remote server or HPC, where there may be no IDE;
they are easy to copy into a README so others can follow them.

Use whichever you find faster day to day. What matters is that the environment is recorded in a file that is stored with your project.

title: Course notes
text:
3.9 Learn more about environments

uv: Python projects and environments.
renv: R environments.
Effective Python environment management: venv and conda.
Managing dependencies with uv and pixi.

title: Course notes
text:
Exercise






NoteExercise



Follow the steps for your language. Do this if your tools are set up.








Step
Python
R




1 Create the environment
uv init
renv::init()


2 Add a package
uv add pandas
install.packages("ggplot2"), then renv::snapshot()


3 Look at the lock file
uv.lock
renv.lock


4 Delete the environment
delete .venv
delete renv/library


5 Restore it
uv sync
renv::restore()



No code? Write your program and its version in your README.
Extra: zip the project without the environment folder, and swap with a neighbour to rebuild it.








CautionAnswer (click to open)






The pyproject.toml / renv.lock file lists your packages. The lock file also records exact versions.
After deleting the environment folder and running uv sync or renv::restore(), the packages are installed again. This is the point of a disposable environment: the folder and its lock file are all you need to share.
For the spreadsheet, the README note is the equivalent. It will not install anything, but it tells the next person what you used.










TipKey points




Use a separate environment for every project.
Record it in a lock file and keep that file with your code.
An environment should be disposable and easy to recreate.
Send the lock file, not the environment: your colleague can rebuild it with one command.
The CLI and IDE do the same thing: use what suits you.

title: Course notes
text:
4.1 Q-FAIR data principles
The FAIR principles are a well-known checklist for sharing data. Q-FAIR adds Quality at the start:









Letter
Principle
What it means in practice
Where we met it




Q
Data Quality
Data is accurate, complete and documented. You know where it came from and what was done to it.
Raw data is never overwritten; the pipeline records every change.


F
Findable
People, and computers, can find it. It has a clear name and description.
Clear folder layout and a README.


A
Accessible
It is clear how to get the data, and under what conditions.
README setup and access notes.


I
Interoperable
It uses open, standard formats that other tools can read.
See “Four things to do”.


R
Reusable
Others can understand and re-use it, with a clear licence.
See “Four things to do”.

title: Course notes
text:
4.2 Why it matters

Funders and journals increasingly expect data to be shared.
Others can build on your work, and check it.
Future you can find and understand your own data.
Your work gets cited.

title: Course notes
text:
4.3 Four things to do
1. Use open file formats. Share data as CSV (comma-separated values), which is plain text that every tool can read, rather than a format that needs one program. In Excel, use File > Save As and choose CSV UTF-8. A CSV holds one sheet only, and keeps values, not formulas.
2. Describe your data. Write a data dictionary, with one row per column, as in the Documentation section, and keep it next to the data.
3. Add a licence. Without one, others don’t know whether they can reuse your work. Common choices are CC BY 4.0 for data and text, and MIT for code. The Creative Commons chooser and choosealicense.com can help. Your funder or institution may have requirements, so check first.
4. Deposit it. Put the data in a repository that gives it a permanent home and a DOI (a persistent identifier you can cite), such as Zenodo, your institution’s data repository (at Bristol this is data.bris), or one specific to your field.
Sensitive data. Some data can’t be shared openly, for example because it contains personal information. You can usually still share the metadata (the README and data dictionary) and explain how others can apply for access. Check with your research data team or ethics committee before depositing anything involving people.

title: Course notes
text:
4.4 Where next?

The FAIR principles and The Turing Way guide to research data management: community guides to sharing data, in depth.
Bristol Training courses: including Intermediate R, Intermediate Python and Best Practices in Software Engineering.
Version control with git lets you go back to a version that worked, develop new features in branches, and collaborate. Use it for every project. We cover it in a separate git and GitHub course.
Functions and testing make analysis code easier to read and trust. See the Bristol and Turing Way courses above.

Getting the balance right is hard: do what you can. You learn by doing, so try to put one or two of these ideas into your next project.

title: Course notes
text:
Exercise






NoteExercise



Pick a dataset: the penguins data from the demos, or one of your own. For each letter of Q-FAIR, write down one thing the data already does well and one thing you could improve.








CautionAnswer (click to open)





There is no single right answer. Typical improvements are:

Q: keep raw data read-only and describe each cleaning step.
F: add a README and give files descriptive names.
A: say where the data is stored and who can use it, or how to request access if it is restricted.
I: save data as CSV rather than a proprietary format.
R: add a data dictionary and a licence.










TipKey points




Q-FAIR: data Quality, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable.
Share data in open formats such as CSV, with a data dictionary and a licence.
Deposit it in a repository that gives it a DOI.
If data can’t be shared, share the metadata and explain how to ask for access.

text:
Why bother?


Future you Code written as if others will use it is easier to return to after a holiday, or in six months’ time


Speed A project set up as a pipeline can be re-run quickly when the data changes or a reviewer asks for something new


Confidence You understand how the pieces fit together, and where things might go wrong


Sharing and careers Journals and funders increasingly expect shared code and data, and tidy work is easy to trust



Selfish reasons first: this mostly helps you. Mention the three problems with a messy project: hard to maintain, hard to run somewhere else, hard to understand.

A messy project
my_project/
├── data.csv

│   └── 01_clean_data.R

text:
Think pipeline

Raw data → Clean → Analyse → Outputs


Never overwrite the raw data
Save useful intermediate outputs
Anything in outputs/ can be re-created by running the code


Excel users: same idea. Raw file untouched, a working copy, one named sheet per step, and a README describing each step.

Comments are for people reading the code, the README is for people running it, the data dictionary is for people using the data, and external documentation is for people who may never see the code. title: Reproducible Research
text:
What is Quarto?




Write text and code in one file (report.qmd)
Render it into a report: HTML, PDF or Word
The code runs when you render, so the results come from the code
Works with R, Python and more, in the IDE you already use
Free and open source: quarto.org




report.qmd


↓ render


report.html



Quarto is the tool this whole course is built with: the slides, the notes and the website are all Quarto. It is free, and works with R, Python and Julia.

title: Reproducible Research
text:
Why Quarto for reproducible research?


No copy and paste Numbers, tables and figures come straight from the code, so they can’t drift out of sync with the analysis


Always up to date If the data changes, render again and the whole report updates


One source, many outputs The same file can make HTML, PDF, Word, slides and websites


Plain text Easy to share, compare and keep in version control, in any editor



The key idea is that the report is the analysis. A reader, or you in six months, can see exactly how every number was produced, and re-create it.

title: Reproducible Research
section: The old way vs the Quarto way
text:
The old way vs the Quarto way


Without Quarto


Run the analysis
Copy numbers and plots into a Word document
The data changes
Repeat by hand, and hope you caught every number



With Quarto


Write the report once, with the code in it
Render
The data changes
Render again

title: Reproducible Research
text:
Weaving text and analysis together



---
title: "Penguin report"
format: html
---

## Data

```{r}
clean <- read.csv("data/processed/penguins_clean.csv")
```

There are `{r} nrow(clean)` penguins in the data.



Header: the title and the output format
Text: ordinary Markdown, with headings and lists
Code chunk: the code runs when you render, and its output appears underneath
Inline code: a result inside a sentence




The header is written between two lines of three dashes in a real file. Point at each part in turn. Inline code is the clever bit: the number in the sentence is calculated every time the report is rendered.

title: Reproducible Research
section: If the data changes, the report updates
text:
If the data changes, the report updates

New data → Re-run the cleaning → Render → Updated report



Every number, table and figure is recalculated
Sentences with inline code update too
There is nothing to copy and paste



✔ Change the data (or the code), not the report

title: Reproducible Research
text:
Quarto can do much more


Reports HTML, PDF and Word documents, with tables, figures and references


Slides This deck is a Quarto presentation


Websites This course website is built with Quarto


Papers and books Journal articles, theses and books, with citations and cross-references

Rendering

title: Reproducible Research
text:
Exercise 2: what good looks like


You could say what would change before you rendered, and why
Only the results changed: no copying and pasting was needed
A README answers three questions in the first minute: what is this project and is it finished? What do I do first? What do I need installed?
A data dictionary has a plain-English description, units and missing-value codes for every column

title: Reproducible Research
text:
Learn more about Quarto


Get started and the guide
Using code: R, Python and inline code
Output formats, websites and presentations
The Quarto gallery: examples to copy from

title: Reproducible Research
text:
The problem: “it worked last year”

Last year: your analysis runs, using version 1.2 of a package
This year: a new project needs version 1.3, so you update
You re-run last year’s analysis: it breaks, or gives different results 💥


Your computer has one shared set of packages, so two projects that need different versions can’t both be happy


Everyone who has coded for a while has had this. The same code, a different version of a package, and a different result, or an error. Ask who has had it.

title: Reproducible Research
text:
Why does this happen?


Packages change Functions are renamed, defaults change and bugs are fixed


Your code depends on them The same code with a different package version can give a different result


Other computers differ A colleague, a new laptop or an HPC: “it works on my machine”


Nothing records it Your project doesn’t say which versions it needs, so nobody can tell what went wrong

title: Reproducible Research
text:
What is an environment?


Without environments

One shared library of packages for every project on your computer


With environments

Each project has its own set of packages, at the versions it needs



Project 1 → package v1.2


Project 2 → package v1.3


An environment is a project’s own folder of installed packages. Projects can no longer interfere with each other, and each one has what it needs.

title: Reproducible Research
text:
How do environments work?

Lock file → Create the environment → Packages installed



The lock file is the recipe: an exact list of packages and versions. It is small, and you keep it with your project
The environment is what gets built from it: the installed packages, in their own folder
Your code only sees the packages in its own environment
The environment is disposable: delete it, and rebuild it from the lock file whenever you like

title: Reproducible Research
text:
The tools





Python
R




Tool
uv
renv


Lock file (keep it)
uv.lock
renv.lock


Environment (disposable)
.venv
renv/library


Rebuild it
uv sync
renv::restore()





Other tools do the same job: venv, conda and pixi for Python, and conda or pixi for R. The idea is the same whichever you use: a file that records what the project needs.

title: Reproducible Research
section: Send your project to someone, and it works
text:
Send your project to someone, and it works

Your project + lock file → Colleague rebuilds the environment → Same packages, same results




✔ Send: your code, README and lock file (and the data, if you can)



✘ Don’t send: the environment itself. It is large, and specific to your computer



This is the payoff. The lock file travels with the project, by email, zip or git. Your colleague, a reviewer, or you on a new laptop runs one command and gets the same packages. You can send it to a reviewer and it will run first time.

title: Reproducible Research
text:
What environments don’t cover


They record packages. Also write down the version of R or Python in your README (uv can pin Python; renv records the R version but doesn’t install it)
The operating system and hardware can still differ
They don’t include your data



Good enough for almost every project. Perfect is not the goal

title: Reproducible Research
text:
No code? Record it anyway

✔ Write the program, its version and any add-ins in your README: the next person then knows what you used

title: Reproducible Research
text:
Live demo 4: An environment
Live demo I do · 8 min · Terminal and console


Create the environment, and add a package
Look at the lock file
Delete the environment, then restore it, as a colleague would



STOP HERE and switch to the demo. Do R in the example project, and Python in a scratch folder: (R) renv::init(), install a package, renv::snapshot(), open renv.lock, delete renv/library, renv::restore(); (Python) uv init, uv add pandas, open pyproject.toml and uv.lock, delete .venv, uv sync. When you delete and restore, say “this is what your colleague does when you send them the project”. Note that renv records package versions but not the version of R itself. This is a demo only: attendees try it in the exercise, if their tools are set up. If your audience is only R or only Python, do just that tool.

title: Reproducible Research
text:
IDE vs CLI


In your IDE

Create a project from a template
Buttons and panels
Different in every IDE


On the command line

uv init, uv add, renv::init()
Same everywhere, including HPC
Easy to copy into a README



Spend about two minutes here. Show where your IDE creates a project with an environment (in Positron: New Folder from Template), then say that theirs will have something similar. Stress that the file is what matters, not how you made it.

Step
Python

About 7 minutes, if your tools are set up. Answers on the next slide, and in the notes.

title: Reproducible Research
text:
Exercise 3: what you should see


pyproject.toml / renv.lock list your packages. The lock file also records exact versions
After deleting the environment folder, uv sync / renv::restore() installs everything again: that is what “disposable” means
The README note does the same job for spreadsheets: it tells the next person what you used
This is what a colleague does when you send them your project: one command to get the same packages

title: Reproducible Research
text:
Q-FAIR data principles


Quality Accurate, complete, documented


Findable Clear names and description


Accessible Clear how to get it


Interoperable Open, standard formats


Reusable Documented, with a licence



Read more: the FAIR principles


Link Q, F and A back to earlier sections (read-only raw data, README, setup notes). The next slides cover I and R. Keep this section brisk: it is a signpost, not a tutorial.

title: Reproducible Research
text:
Why it matters


Funders and journals increasingly expect data to be shared
Others can build on your work, and check it
Future you can find and understand your own data
Your work gets cited



Quality comes first: there is no point sharing data that nobody can trust or understand.

title: Reproducible Research
text:
Four things to do





What to do
Learn more




Open formats
Share data as CSV, not a format that needs one program
Turing Way: research data management


Describe it
Write a data dictionary: what each column means, its units and missing values
See section 2


Add a licence
Data: CC BY 4.0. Code: MIT
Creative Commons chooser, choosealicense.com


Deposit it
A repository that gives a DOI, such as Zenodo or your institution’s
Zenodo





Can’t share the data? Share the README and data dictionary, and explain how to ask for access


Open formats: in Excel use File > Save As > CSV UTF-8, one sheet per file, and note that formulas become values. A data dictionary has one row per column, as in section 2. Check funder and institution requirements for licences. Refer ethics and consent questions to the research data team.

text:
Exercise 4: a Q-FAIR check ✍️


Pick a dataset: the penguins data from the demos, or one of your own.
For each letter of Q-FAIR, write down:

one thing the data already does well
one thing you could improve




About 5 minutes. Example answer on the next slide.

title: Reproducible Research
text:
Exercise 4: what good looks like


Q: keep raw data read-only; describe each cleaning step
F: add a README; descriptive file names
A: say where it is stored and who can use it
I: save as CSV
R: add a data dictionary and a licence

title: Reproducible Research
text:
What you can now do


✔ Organise a project, and never edit the raw data
✔ Write a README and a data dictionary
✔ Build a Quarto report that updates when the data changes
✔ Record the software a project needs, so it can be re-run anywhere
✔ Check data against Q-FAIR, and know where to find out more



A project that does all of this is already most of the way to reproducible
